scenes.say: Two reviewers read the same model answer. One scores it a four. The other scores it a two. By the end, you'll grade so both agree, then judge an agent by its steps.
Today you will do three things. Grade answers with a rubric that two people share. Compare two answers when no checklist fits. And judge an agent by every step it took.
lines: Grade with a rubric two people share
Compare A and B when no checklist fits
Judge an agent by every step it took

scenes.title: Explain recursion: 4 or 2?
scenes.statement: Two model answers to 'explain recursion'. Score each from 0 to 5, so that any two graders give the same score.

example.input: Answer A and Answer B, two graders
example.output: Both graders: A is 4, B is 2

scenes.say: Here is the problem. Two answers to explain recursion, two graders. For example, answers A and B. We want both graders to agree: four for A, two for B.

scenes.head: Why a noisy score hurts
scenes.say: Why care? A team ships whichever model scores higher. If the same answer gets a four from one grader and a two from another, the ranking is noise. Noise picks the wrong model, and users get the worse one.

scenes.head: A rubric is a mark scheme
scenes.say: Think of marking an exam. Ask two teachers, is this a good essay, and they give two different grades. Hand them a mark scheme, two points for this, two points for that, and they land on the same grade. The rubric is the mark scheme.

scenes.head: Our rubric and two answers
scenes.say: Here is our rubric, out of five. Correct is worth up to two: no false claims. Complete, up to two: names the self call and the base case. Clear, one. Answer A is correct and clear, but never names a base case. Answer B calls recursion a loop.

panels.code:
Correct   0-2: no false claim
Complete  0-2: self-call and
          base case named
Clear     0-1: easy to follow

Total: 0 to 5

A: A function that calls
   itself on a smaller input.
   Example: 3! is 3 times 2!

B: A loop that repeats some
   code.

scenes.head: Two graders, same scores
scenes.say: Two graders, two answers, one rubric. Grader one scores answer A at four. Grader two gives it four again. Now answer B. Grader one gives two. Grader two gives two as well. Keep A and B as anchors, worked examples of a four and a two.
Your turn. A new answer says: recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller input until a base case stops it. Apply the rubric. What score? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Answer C: 'A function calls itself on a smaller input until a base case stops it.'

scenes.head: Scoring answer C
scenes.say: Five. Correct earns two, nothing false. Complete earns two, it names the self call and the base case. Clear earns one. No example needed, because the rubric never asked for one.

chapters.title: Pass or fail, one check each

scenes.title: Exactly two sentences
scenes.statement: The prompt says: summarize in exactly two sentences, no bullets. The response reads well. Does it pass?

example.output: Fail: it broke an explicit rule

scenes.say: Next problem. The prompt wants exactly two sentences. The response reads well. For example, it has three short ones. Does it pass? No, it broke a rule. A quick reader misses that.

scenes.head: A prompt and its response
scenes.say: Here is the prompt, and the response. Read the response. Smooth, and every fact matches. Now count the sentences. One, two, three. A quick reader says good summary. A careful grader sees a broken rule.

panels.code:
Summarize in exactly
two sentences.
No bullets.

Text: The city opened a
new bridge on Monday. It
cuts commutes by 12 min
and cost 40 million.

panels.label: 3 sentences
panels.code:
The city opened a bridge.
It cuts commutes by 12
minutes.
It cost 40 million dollars.

scenes.head: Four checks, pass or fail
scenes.say: A rubric splits one vague question into small checks. Facts match the text: pass. Rules followed: fail, three sentences. Nothing invented: pass. Clear and short: pass. Each check is pass or fail, so graders have little room to disagree, and you can say exactly why points were lost.
Your turn. Same two sentence summary, but now the response says the bridge cost four hundred million. The text said forty. Which check fails? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: The text says 40 million; the response says 400 million. Which check fails?

scenes.head: Four checks, pass or fail
scenes.say: Facts match fails. The text says forty million, and the response says four hundred million. Rules followed now passes. Nothing invented still passes, because only a number is wrong. One failed check, one reason.

scenes.head: Three grading traps
scenes.say: Three traps. Rewarding length: longer wins by habit. Rewarding tone: a warm wrong answer is still wrong. Writing only good: say which check failed, so others can repeat it.

chapters.title: No checklist? Compare A and B

scenes.title: Which reply sounds better?
scenes.statement: Two replies to an angry customer. No checklist captures sounds better. How do you pick a winner that holds up?

example.input: Reply A vs Reply B, same prompt
example.output: A winner plus a written reason

scenes.say: No checklist. Which of two replies to an angry customer sounds better? For example, reply A against reply B. We want a winner, and a written reason.

scenes.head: Pairwise: a blind taste test
scenes.say: Think of a blind taste test. Nobody scores flavor. You taste two cups, pick one, say why. Answers work the same: two answers, a winner, a reason.

scenes.head: Judge twice, swap the order
scenes.say: Graders tend to favor whatever they see first. That is position bias, so judge twice. Run one: A in the first slot, B second. The grader picks A. Run two: swap them. B first, A second. It picks A again. Same winner in both orders, so we trust it.
Your turn. Order A then B, and the grader picks A. Swap to B then A, and it picks B. What does that tell you? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Order A,B picks A. Order B,A picks B. What happened?

scenes.head: Both orders, or it's a tie
scenes.say: Position bias: it picked the first slot twice. This code asks in both orders. If the picks disagree, it says tie. Our biased judge always says slot one, so it says tie. A fair judge would not.

scenes.head: Follow-ups you'll hear
scenes.say: Three follow-ups. When two graders still disagree, fix the rubric, then re-grade. Can a model grade for you? Yes, but spot check its scores against humans. Why write a reason? So another person can check and repeat it.
rows: Others can check and repeat it

chapters.title: Grade the route, not the end

scenes.title: Cheapest flight to Boston
scenes.statement: An agent must book the cheapest flight to Boston on May 3. It makes five tool calls, then says: Booked!

example.input: 5 tool calls, then 'Booked the cheapest flight!'
example.output: Score every step, not the message

scenes.say: Now the model acts. It must book the cheapest Boston flight. For example, five tool calls, then a cheerful message. We must grade the whole run.

scenes.head: A driving test
scenes.say: Think of a driving test. A driver arrives on time, but ran a red light on the way. The examiner still fails them, because the route matters. An agent is a model that takes actions by calling tools, like search or payment. So we grade the route too, not only the arrival.

scenes.head: The trajectory: five tool calls
scenes.say: That run is the trajectory: every tool call, in order. Step one searches flights for May three. Step two sorts by price. Step three books a flight. Step four charges the card. Step five tells the user. Looks fine, until you read step three.

scenes.head: Score every step
scenes.say: Now score each step on its own. Search for May three: pass. Sort by price: pass. Booking: fail. It picked May four. Charging the card paid for the wrong flight. The reply sounds right but is false. The outcome check agrees: wrong date.

scenes.head: The outcome check, as code
scenes.say: Here is the outcome check, written as code. It reads the real booking from the database, not the agent's message. Right day? Cheapest price? Charged exactly once? All three must hold. For our run the day is May four, so it prints False.

panels.code:
def passed(db):
    b = db.booking()
    right_day = b.date == "May 3"
    cheapest = b.price == db.cheapest("May 3")
    once = db.charges() == 1
    return right_day and cheapest and once

print(passed(db))

setup.check.py:
class B: pass
class DB:
    def booking(s):
        b = B(); b.date = "May 4"; b.price = 212; return b
    def cheapest(s, d): return 212
    def charges(s): return 1
db = DB()

scenes.say: Your turn. Agent A and agent B both book the right flight, on the right day, at the cheapest price. But agent B also deleted the user's saved trips on the way. Who passes? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A and B both book it right. B also deletes saved trips. Who passes?

scenes.head: Outcome plus route
scenes.say: Only A passes. Both outcomes pass, but B's route did damage nobody asked for. Check the route for side effects.

scenes.head: Four agent-grading mistakes
scenes.say: Four mistakes. Grading the final message only? Check the real state and the tool calls. Demanding one exact path? Accept any route that passes. A flaky tool? Run it several times, report the pass rate. Letting the agent edit the check? Lock it, and fail runs that touch it.
rows: Run several times, report pass rate
Let the agent edit the check
Lock it; fail runs that touch it

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you grade consistently? Use separate checks with anchored examples. No clean checklist? Compare A and B, swap the order, and write why. Graders disagree? Fix the rubric, then re-grade. A model as grader? Yes, but spot check against humans.
rows: Compare A and B, swap order, say why

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you evaluate an agent? Check the outcome with code. What's on the route? Tool calls, arguments, side effects. Many valid paths? Accept any that pass. Flaky tool? Run several times. Cheating? Lock the checks.
rows: Code check on the final state
Check the outcome, not exact steps
Run several times, report pass rate
Lock the check; flag edits to it

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Try these three. First, write a rubric for a two sentence summary. Grade five answers with a friend. Second, judge ten answer pairs in both orders and count the flips. Third, write a code check for the flight task that reads the final state.
